I went to Xavier Prep and I met one of my oldest friends, Mr. Clyde Cuss, Sr. He was teaching at Xavier Prep at the time. I was in a band. And he used to come in the classroom and do a lot of writing, writing for bands. He had a band and a group. And he was writing. And this was my first experience as far as arranging is concerned. Yeah. How did you go from that big band concept to a really just a very simple rhythmic?

Well, let me see what I'll give it to myself. It ain't no secret. Big band and small band is the same, it's the same thing to me. It's just that you hear more color in big band than you do with a smaller group, but the arranging technique is practically the same. You understand, with the exception, if you have three trumpets, you would give them something different than what you would have on the, like if I was to rearrange some of these songs that's on the air that don't have any horns, period, then I'd adopt them to my big band, which I do anyway. And it's the idea of hearing one thing and then add it on from that particular melody. And where the color come in is that I'll take what the, maybe what the violin would do, I might give it to a trumpet here, and what the violin is doing there, I might get to the reeds here, that's different colorization. But voicing is the same no matter what instrument you write for. For instance, another example, if you write for strings, and you see 45 people, in the strings, well how do you write for 45 people? You don't. You write for four people, and you have five, you have 10 to 20 people playing one part. You understand? Some people think, well man how can you write for 40 strings? You're not, you know. Your horns is a different story, you write for the amount of horns that you have. But strings is the same thing. Now the technique of writing is different, you know, because strings, when you have such a broad spectrum from here to here, you have to know what you're doing because you have so many overtones that you have to consider things like that.
The viola to the cellos.
Yeah, to the strings, to the top strings and all that kind of stuff. But basically it's the same. I hate to say that because some people...

But it also, it seems to me that the technology was able by the late 60s, early 70s, to enhance the bass, say bass and drums. Mm-hmm. To where you can do some simpler things. Yeah. You can, you know, the studio can embellish those instruments.

Yeah, but they only can embellish what you're playing. Mm-hmm. Yeah, they might give you some different sound from what you're playing. Right. You understand? Yeah. You know, so maybe that's what you mean, it's something like that. But anyway, then came, I started working with different artists. Through the years I got a reputation, so now I'm getting more work now than I have. Right now? Yeah. I mean, more larger artists than I like.
Who have you been working with lately? I haven't.

Well, you heard about the Bobby Robinson thing. I did an album with them. It was this Bobby Robinson. They did it in New Orleans too. It was like a Mardi Gras type stuff, the album is. We did a video. I was on the video at the Margarita. I did something with Mark Cohen, Fats Domino, Dave, DeVell, Johnny Adams, I'm a Thomas. Well, I didn't do no. I just do a head, a band arrangement, stage arrangement. I'm doing the Neville Brothers, really this week, starting this week.
For a new album they're working on? Yeah. It's the Neville Brothers, not Aaron? I think it's A&M.
No, it's the Neville Brothers. Yeah.
Because Aaron usually does his thing. Yeah.
I don't know if he's going to be on this. I don't know. But he usually, some of them are on all of them.
Well, but they separate between an Aaron project and a Neville Brothers project.
Neville Brothers, yeah. But I mean, he'd be on the project with them. Yeah, he'd be on the project. I have him. I got, uh.
Didn't you do something recently with Charles Brown? Something with Charles Brown?

I did an album with Charles. I did a tour with him. Charles Brown's album must have been about two, three years ago. I did something in Washington, D.C. We did a concert from the album in Oakland, California, the Oakland Symphony. I wrote for that. Oh, man. I know there's somebody in between. But I still can do it. Oh, it's obvious.

Yeah. Yeah. Um. We're almost finished with this reel. Uh. Well, we can leave it at that. At some point, if I ever, we want to do another follow up at some point. Call me. There's some things, there's a few things here we didn't get to, but we can, you know, at some point. Oh, I wanted to do that.
Yeah. For more information visit www.fema.org

segments.title: Opening: date and birthplace question
segments.summary: Interviewer confirms the date and asks for birthday and birthplace.

segments.title: Musical family in New Orleans and early arranging with Clyde Kerr
segments.summary: Born 1930 in New Orleans into a musical family; plays trumpet professionally from 12-13; learns arranging from Clyde Kerr Sr. at Xavier Prep and from stock arrangements, and forms a trio with the Johnson brothers.

segments.title: Family band and Sunday jam sessions
segments.summary: Quezergue says he played trumpet, learned reading through the family orchestra and Mr. Kerr, and describes the Sunday family jam sessions; the ASR degenerates into a loop.

segments.title: Reel changes and photograph shown
segments.summary: Tape announcements for reels two and three, with a photograph from the Lehman Brothers mentioned.

segments.title: Dave Bartholomew's trust and who gets producer credit
segments.summary: Quezergue discusses working for Dave, who gave him tasks but stayed in the studio; he complains that money-men get producer credit over the person doing the work.

segments.title: Work after Imperial and the introduction to Malaco
segments.summary: After Imperial he worked with local people, then met Walker, who connected him with Malaco Records in Mississippi, leading to Mr. Big Stuff.

segments.title: The NOLA label photo: officers and Quezergue's role
segments.summary: Looking at a 1962 photo, he lists NOLA's officers and attorney and says he was arranger and recording director, unsure of timing relative to Mr. Big Stuff.

segments.title: Sequence of Dave, NOLA Records and Malaco
segments.summary: Sorting out the order: Dave first, then NOLA Records with Barefootin', Trick Bag and a June Gardner album, all before Malaco.

segments.title: How NOLA and Malaco sessions were financed; Barefootin' origins
segments.summary: Partners paid for sessions, musicians were paid more after hits; Robert Parker brought the song Barefootin', which sat on the shelf and was released on Eugene Welly's label.

segments.title: Atlantic Records confusion over Barefootin'
segments.summary: Atlantic thought Barefootin' was theirs under a deal; threats of a lawsuit came to nothing, and NOLA distributed it itself.

segments.title: After Barefootin': Dave, then Malaco with Jean Knight and King Floyd
segments.summary: Chronology after Barefootin': work with Dave, then the Malaco material with Jean Knight and King Floyd.

segments.title: Getting involved with the Dixie Cups through Joe Jones
segments.summary: Joe Jones brought the Dixie Cups to him, and they went to New York where Jones talked his way into a Leiber and Stoller studio session, getting the group signed.

segments.title: Arranging Chapel of Love and the Dixie Cups' songs
segments.summary: He did the horn arrangements on their records but did not produce Chapel of Love; he cannot recall whether he changed its ballad concept.

segments.title: Reworking Groove Me for King Floyd without the producer's knowledge
segments.summary: He fixes raw songs with changes; Groove Me was arranged on the way from hotel to studio, cut without King Floyd present, and he got no percentage.

segments.title: Malaco, Chimneyville and the Stax and Atlantic tape
segments.summary: Chimneyville was a Malaco subsidiary on a percentage deal; the tape with Groove Me and Mr. Big Stuff was sent to labels, Groove Me was released independently, and Atlantic and Stax took notice.

segments.title: Mr. Big Stuff and the James Brown band who found it too simple
segments.summary: He added the instrumental middle and bass line and arranged horns; at the Apollo James Brown's band took two hours to learn the simple song.

segments.title: Song credits for arrangers
segments.summary: He declined a song credit on Mr. Big Stuff, taking producer credit and half the royalties instead, and says arranging changes alone do not merit songwriting shares.

segments.title: From big band to tight rhythm records; arranging technique and studio technology
segments.summary: He says big band and small band arranging are the same technique with different colour, discusses writing for strings, and says the studio can only embellish what is played.

segments.title: Recent projects: Mardi Gras album and the Neville Brothers
segments.summary: Recent work includes a Mardi Gras album with Johnny Adams, Fats Domino and others, and a coming Neville Brothers album.

segments.title: Charles Brown album, tour and Oakland Symphony concert
segments.summary: He made an album and toured with Charles Brown and wrote for an Oakland Symphony concert.

segments.title: Closing the reel
segments.summary: The interviewer wraps up, proposing a follow-up interview; the ASR trails into noise.
